notes.text: Santa Parade: the start time and meeting point are not announced yet, and sign-up only opens in early November. Register all 8 the day it opens, then move the afternoon to the real slot.
Passports and the JR Kansai-Hiroshima Area Pass: today is day 1, so it starts at the first JR gate. The Hankyu and Keihan rides are not JR, so top up your Suica.
A freezing start at Inari and dark well before dinner. Wear layers you can pull a Santa suit over.

stops.summary: Thousands of red gates and nobody in them: climb the torii tunnel while the tour buses are still asleep.
stops.story: Fushimi Inari is a whole mountain lined with vermilion torii, each one paid for by a business hoping for good luck. Get there early in winter and the low sun comes through the gates sideways, the paths are empty and your breath fogs up. Get there late and it's a queue of selfie sticks.
how: Walk out of JR Inari straight through the Rōmon gate and keep going uphill into the Senbon Torii.
Push up to the Yotsutsuji crossroads for the view over Kyoto, then turn back. The full mountain loop is about 4 km and takes 2h+, which you don't have time for.
Be back at the bottom in time for the 2 taxis to Kiyomizu (21 min).
tips: It's quietest from 6 to 9am, and weekends peak 10–16, so the early alarm actually buys you something.
The side paths off the main gate tunnel are where the empty-gate photos are.
It's open 24h and free, so nothing opens late on you.
wishes: We want to maximise all the time we've got in the country
At most two deliberate nights under 4 hours' sleep; any early start after a late night needs a reason (rope-drop at USJ, first light at Fushimi Inari)

stops.summary: A wooden stage hanging over a ravine of bare winter maples, with all of Kyoto spread out below.
stops.story: Kiyomizu's main hall sits on a huge wooden scaffold sticking out over the hillside. In December the maples underneath are bare, so you get a clear view all the way across the city. On the way out, the Otowa waterfall splits into three streams, each supposedly good for something different, so pick one and don't be greedy.
how: Pay ¥500 at the gate and head straight for the stage.
Do the main view, then loop down to Otowa-no-taki for one sip each.
Exit downhill. Sannenzaka is an 8-minute walk from the gate.
tips: Open 06:00–18:00 on the trip dates.
A group photo with all 8 is fine, but organised group shoots technically need notice and permission, so keep it quick and don't block the stage.
There's no group discount, so don't bother asking.
wishes: We love to do it all

stops.summary: Stone-stepped lanes of old wooden shops: snack, grab souvenirs, keep walking.
stops.story: Sannenzaka and Ninenzaka are the steep stone lanes that wind down from Kiyomizu toward Yasaka, lined with wooden townhouses that now sell sweets and trinkets. They're touristy, but the shape of the old town is real, and in winter the shopfronts steam with fresh snacks.
how: Walk down from Kiyomizu and follow the slope toward Yasaka Shrine.
Grab yatsuhashi (cinnamon rice-dough sweets) and look into the Starbucks in an old townhouse, with tatami rooms upstairs.
Carry on via Yasaka and Shijō-dōri, over the Kamo river, to Nishiki.
tips: This is a snack-and-go stop, not a shopping stop. The real shopping is in Osaka.
Legend says if you trip on Sannenzaka you'll have bad luck, so watch the steps.
wishes: We love to do it all

stops.summary: Kyoto's 400m food street: lunch is whatever you point at, stall by stall.
stops.story: Nishiki is a narrow covered arcade packed with stalls that have fed Kyoto kitchens for generations: rolled tamagoyaki, baby octopus with a quail egg stuffed in its head, soy-milk doughnuts, pickles of every colour. Eight people splitting skewers down the length of it is the best lunch in the city.
how: Go in from one end and work your way along. Most bites cost ¥300–800.
Eat at the stall where you bought it. Walking while eating is frowned on here.
Leave from Karasuma for the Hankyu limited express at 13:31, which reaches Osaka-umeda at 14:13 (¥410, on Suica, not the JR pass).
tips: Budget about ¥2,000 each and stop before you're full. The Santa Parade comes next.
Stall hours vary, roughly 10:00–17:00, and some close Wednesdays and Sundays. Tuesday is fine.
Must-try: tako-tamago and the soy-milk doughnuts.
wishes: We love to do it all
We want to maximise all the time we've got in the country

stops.summary: Eight of you join a horde of Santas parading through Umeda, and you keep the suits.
stops.story: Every December the Umekita district behind Osaka Station fills with hundreds of people in Santa suits, mostly office workers from the two big complexes, handing out presents and cleaning the streets as they go. It's free, the costume is yours to keep, and nobody at home will believe you. The parade is confirmed for Tuesday 22 December 2026.
how: Sign up: recruitment opens in early November on the GRAND FRONT OSAKA and GRAND GREEN OSAKA sites. Register all 8 on day one.
The start time and meeting point are not announced yet. Don't trust the time on this card until the confirmation comes through.
Check in, suit up, parade through Umekita handing out presents, and keep the suits for Christmas Day.
tips: In 2025 it was free with 500 public places, first come first served, and sign-up closed on 15 Dec or when full. Assume it will fill early.
If you miss out, buy Santa suits at Donki and spend this time at LUCUA and Nintendo OSAKA, then the tree show.
Keep the suits clean: they're your Christmas Day outfit.
stops.cost: Free (2025 terms; suit is yours to keep)
stops.booking: Sign-up opens early November on the GRAND FRONT OSAKA / GRAND GREEN OSAKA sites; register all 8 the day it opens
stops.hours: Start time and meeting point not yet announced
wishes: The Grand Santa Parade in Umekita, Osaka (about 500 Santas, suits provided and yours to keep; needs a sign-up; Plan C had it on Tue 22 Dec)
Christmas Day in Santa suits, the whole group, ending in a Round1 all-nighter in Osaka
Be bold: prefer one-of-a-kind, local-run, hard-to-book and group-scale things, and name a safe fallback beside every hard-to-book thing

stops.summary: Still in the suits: a light show on the giant tree and the group photo under gold-lit Umekita.
stops.story: It's already dark by now, and Grand Front's North Building tree runs a light show while the Umekita lawn glows champagne gold. On its own it's just a mall tree. With eight sweaty Santas in front of it, it's the photo of the trip.
how: Walk 4 min from the parade to the North Building tree.
Shows run on the hour and at 15, 30 and 45 past, so you'll never wait long.
Take the group photo, then head to Hankyu Osaka-umeda for the 17:44 limited express, which reaches Kyoto-kawaramachi at 18:28 (¥410).
tips: The lights run 16:00–24:00 today, so if the parade runs late you won't miss them.
The show times come from a third-party event site, so take whatever slot you get.
wishes: Christmas Day in Santa suits, the whole group, ending in a Round1 all-nighter in Osaka

stops.summary: Willows, a stone canal and teahouse lanterns: Kyoto's prettiest street, after dark.
stops.story: Shirakawa is a short stretch of canal lined with willows and wooden teahouses, with little Tatsumi Bridge and its shrine in the middle. The glow comes from the teahouse lanterns and street lamps, not a festival, and on a December night it's cold, quiet and almost too pretty to be real.
how: From Kawaramachi, cross the Shijō bridge into Gion and find Tatsumi-bashi.
Group photo on the bridge, then walk the canal.
Cut down Hanamikoji and over Shijō-ōhashi into Pontochō, a 9-minute walk.
tips: People live in these teahouses, so keep the noise way down.
Don't chase or close-up photograph geiko or maiko.
wishes: If there are cool nightlife things to do in the neighbouring cities as well, include them

stops.summary: Duck hot-pot for 8 on tatami in an old Pontochō townhouse.
stops.story: Robin serves kamo-nabe, duck simmered at the table in a rich broth, inside a 150-year-old townhouse on Kyoto's lantern-lit drinking alley. After a day of Santa suits and stairs, sitting on the floor around a bubbling pot is exactly right.
how: Book the 19:15 slot on TableCheck: duck hot-pot course ¥9,200 pp, plus ¥550 pp for the private room.
Ask for the zashiki (tatami room) for all 8, because the table rooms only seat 2–6.
Order your last drinks before the 20:30 last order.
tips: If you can't get the zashiki, don't split up. Fall back to walk-in izakaya on Kiyamachi.
Kiyamachi is a 4-minute walk away once you're done.
stops.booking: TableCheck, duck hot-pot course; request the zashiki for 8 (8名で、個室)
wishes: Everyone stays together; every booking is for 8 at the same table or private room (8名で、同じテーブル/個室)

stops.summary: Kyoto's cheap, young canal-side bar strip: two rounds, then the last good train home.
stops.story: Pontochō is where Kyoto drinks expensively. One block west, Kiyamachi is where it drinks cheaply: standing bars, chain bars, international bars and karaoke along a narrow canal between Shijō and Sanjō. It's the student end of town, which makes it your end of town.
how: Walk one block west, 4 min.
Do two rounds. Beers are about ¥500–700 and cocktails about ¥800–1,200.
Leave by 22:30 and walk to Sanjō for the 22:50 Keihan to Kitahama, then Metro via Sakaisuji-Hommachi to Kujō at 23:57 (¥730).
tips: It's cheaper than Pontochō for the same drinks.
Small bars might not seat 8, so split across two next door to each other rather than leave anyone behind.
Miss the 22:50 and the backup is Hankyu from Kawaramachi to Umeda. A taxi straight home takes 60 min and costs a lot.
wishes: If there are cool nightlife things to do in the neighbouring cities as well, include them
Karaoke (Manekineko, Big Echo, Karaokekan), arcades, izakaya and yokocho nights, standing bars, and the last-train problem solved properly
